title: Data centre builders pre-order generators two years ahead
source_used: ET Datacenters (full text, fetched directly because the shared fulltext copy was empty)
key_facts: Data-centre builders are ordering generators two years in advance and committing to suppliers before final designs are complete, according to speakers at the Capacity Europe 2026 conference (ET Datacenters).
At a panel on 14 Oct 2026, 'Scaling Under Scarcity: Delivering Projects Amid Shortages', speakers said the focus has moved from negotiating the lowest price to securing manufacturing slots.

Miriam van Kooperen, senior director of supply chain at Greenscale, said high-voltage transformers, gas-insulated switchgear and generator engines are in short supply and the gap between AI development and manufacturing capacity is widening.
Ozgur Duzgunoglu, head of engineering and design at Telehouse, said generators can take two years to arrive and high-voltage transformers 12 to 18 months.

Nelson Pinto de Magalhaes, director of PMO and procurement at Start Campus, said 'Procure first, design around it' is a company mantra and that customers judge operators on meeting the ready-for-service date.

Prefabrication such as off-site-built coolant distribution units is now common to save time; Justin Ryburn of Kentik cited a US data-centre customer running generators continuously until grid power arrives.
Oracle has issued a force majeure notice for Project Jupiter, its Stargate campus in New Mexico, due to potential power supply delays for its 2028 start.

why_it_matters_hint: Shortages of power equipment and skilled labour are pushing data-centre builders to buy equipment years ahead, which shows what limits how fast AI capacity can be built.
